title: Acids and bases: pH, Ka and buffers
note: A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts it; each acid has a conjugate base one proton lighter. pH = −log[H₃O⁺], and at 25 °C Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, so pH + pOH = 14.00. Weak acids ionize partly, measured by Ka. A buffer, a weak acid plus its conjugate base, resists pH change: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

read.title: Protons on the move
text: In the Brønsted–Lowry picture, an acid gives away a proton and a base takes one. When hydrogen fluoride meets water, HF hands a proton to H₂O, forming H₃O⁺ and F⁻. Fluoride is the conjugate base of HF, and hydronium is the conjugate acid of water. Every acid–base reaction is a contest between two such pairs.

Strong acids, such as HCl and HNO₃, give up their protons completely in water. Weak acids, such as HF and acetic acid, react only partly and reach an equilibrium described by Ka. The larger Ka is, the stronger the acid, and the weaker its conjugate base. For any conjugate pair, Ka × Kb equals Kw, 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
The pH scale compresses huge ranges of [H₃O⁺] into small numbers: pH = −log[H₃O⁺]. Each unit is a factor of ten, so a pH 3 solution has 100 times more hydronium than a pH 5 solution.

A buffer holds pH steady. It contains a weak acid and its conjugate base in similar amounts. Added hydroxide is used up by the weak acid, and added hydronium is used up by the base, so the ratio of the two changes only a little. The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), shows that when the two are equal the pH equals the pKa. Blood relies on the carbonic acid and bicarbonate pair.
